claim: Across 15 million PubMed abstracts (2010-2024), certain style words rose abruptly after LLMs appeared, and the excess-word analysis implies at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed (up to 40% in some subcorpora).
quote: This excess word analysis suggests that at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs. This lower bound differed across disciplines, countries, and journals, reaching 40% for some subcorpora.
title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary

claim: In scholarly databases 2022-2024, the term 'delve' rose by 1,500%, 'underscore' by 1,000% and 'intricate' by 700% (Scopus, WoS, PubMed, PMC, Dimensions, OpenAlex).
quote: Across databases, delve (+ 1,500%), underscore (+ 1,000%), and intricate (+ 700%) had the largest increases between 2022 and 2024.
title: How much are LLMs changing the language of academic papers after ChatGPT?

claim: LLM-associated terms co-occur far more in 2024 than 2022 (underscore with pivotal r=0.449, with delve r=0.311, versus 0.032 and 0.018 in 2022), so co-occurrence of several terms is a stronger signal than one word; the authors state the results cannot distinguish LLM-generated from LLM-edited text.
quote: in 2024, underscore strongly correlated with pivotal (0.449) and delve (0.311), compared with very weak associations in 2022 (0.032 and 0.018, respectively).
title: How much are LLMs changing the language of academic papers after ChatGPT?

claim: Of 135 candidate AI-influenced terms drawn from 15 studies, 103 showed meaningful increases in PubMed in 2024 (modified Z-score >= 3.5); top increases included delve, underscore, primarily, meticulous, boast. Their rise began around 2020, before ChatGPT's 2022 release.
quote: Of the 135 potentially AI-influenced terms, 103 showed meaningful increases (modified Z-score ≥3.5) in 2024. Terms with the highest increases included "delve," "underscore," "primarily," "meticulous," and "boast."
title: Delving Into PubMed Records: How AI-Influenced Vocabulary has Transformed Medical Writing since ChatGPT

claim: Overuse of flagged words decays once publicised: arXiv abstracts show a marked drop in 'delve' from early 2024, while other ChatGPT-favoured words such as 'significant' kept increasing, so fixed word lists age.
quote: we report a marked drop in the frequency of several words previously identified as overused by ChatGPT, such as "delve", starting soon after they were pointed out in early 2024.
title: Human-LLM Coevolution: Evidence from Academic Writing

claim: A preprint identifies 21 focal words (e.g. delve, intricate, underscore) whose rise in scientific abstracts is likely LLM-driven, and finds no evidence that the overrepresentation is caused by architecture, algorithm or training data; RLHF may play a role.
quote: We fail to find evidence that lexical overrepresentation is caused by model architecture, algorithm choices, or training data.
title: Why Does ChatGPT "Delve" So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in Large Language Models

claim: Em-dash prevalence in medRxiv Discussion sections rose from 4.23% before ChatGPT to 11.58% after, and to 20.3% in 2025 (N=69,632 preprints); the author calls it a population-level indicator, not a per-paper detector.
quote: Em-dash prevalence in Discussion sections rose from 4.23% before ChatGPT to 11.58% afterward, an absolute increase of 7.35 percentage points
title: Em-ergence of the em-dash: a population-level rise in em-dash frequency in medRxiv preprints

claim: In a comparison of six LLMs against human news text, human texts had more scattered sentence-length distributions and more varied vocabulary; LLM outputs used more numbers, symbols, auxiliaries and pronouns.
quote: Human texts exhibit more scattered sentence length distributions, more variety of vocabulary, a distinct use of dependency and constituent types, shorter constituents, and more optimized dependency distances.
title: Contrasting Linguistic Patterns in Human and LLM-Generated News Text

claim: In a Japanese study of about 37,000 human/LLM abstract pairs (J-STAGE; GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, two Japanese Llama models), human-written Japanese text used a more diverse vocabulary than LLM-generated text.
quote: it was confirmed that human-written text uses a more diverse vocabulary compared to LLM-generated text.
title: 日本語を対象とした大規模言語モデル生成テキストの識別：データセットの構築と特定のモデルに依存しない分類器の実現

claim: In a controlled experiment, co-writing argumentative essays with InstructGPT (not base GPT-3) raised similarity between different authors' writings and reduced lexical and content diversity (preprint).
quote: it increases the similarity between the writings of different authors and reduces the overall lexical and content diversity.
title: Does Writing with Language Models Reduce Content Diversity?

claim: GPT detectors consistently misclassified non-native English writing samples as AI-generated while native samples were accurately identified, so surface-feature lists risk false positives on plain or constrained human prose.
quote: these detectors consistently misclassify non-native English writing samples as AI-generated, whereas native writing samples are accurately identified.
title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers

claim: Paraphrasing dropped DetectGPT detection accuracy from 70.3% to 4.6% at a constant 1% false positive rate, showing lexical/probabilistic detection is evadable by rewording.
quote: DIPPER drops detection accuracy of DetectGPT from 70.3% to 4.6% (at a constant false positive rate of 1%)
title: Paraphrasing evades detectors of AI-generated text, but retrieval is an effective defense

claim: Five blinded human raters judging article introductions under five AI-use conditions reached 19% overall accuracy, indistinguishable from chance; three online detectors differed in score reliability (ICC 0.57-0.95).
quote: Human scoring was far less consistent, with an overall accuracy of 19%, indistinguishable from chance.
title: Ability of AI detection tools and humans to accurately identify different forms of AI-generated written content

claim: Annotators who frequently use LLMs for writing detected AI articles accurately: the majority vote of five misclassified 1 of 300 English non-fiction articles.
quote: the majority vote among five such "expert" annotators misclassifies only 1 of 300 articles
title: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text

claim: In the same study, expert annotators' free-form explanations show they rely heavily on specific lexical clues but also pick up complex phenomena that automatic detectors find hard to assess.
quote: while they rely heavily on specific lexical clues, they also pick up on more complex phenomena within the text that are challenging to assess for automatic detectors.
title: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text

claim: A rapid review of 40 studies (2022-2026) finds five cue families for AI-versus-human text and no single reliable marker; cue stability is conditional on genre and register.
quote: the literature indicates that AI–human distinction emerges from layered and context-dependent cue profiles rather than from any single reliable marker.
title: What Distinguishes AI-Generated from Human Writing? A Rapid Review of the Literature

claim: Among 16 detectors tested on 42 GPT-3.5, 42 GPT-4 and 42 human essays, most were generally ineffective at separating GPT-4 text from undergraduate writing; three (Copyleaks, TurnItIn, Originality.ai) were accurate on all sets.
quote: they are generally ineffective at distinguishing between GPT-4 papers and those written by undergraduate students.
title: The Effectiveness of Software Designed to Detect AI-Generated Writing: A Comparison of 16 AI Text Detectors
